transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-11-04 16:30 PST
- Duration: ~74 minutes (recorded)
- Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood Infra), Michael Chen (CTO, Glacier), Asha Rao (Platform), Tom Becker (Network), Lance Ho (SRE)

Summary:
Quick but deep session going over private VPC deployment details, egress/NAT tradeoffs, PrivateLink vs public egress, DNS and split-horizon concerns, and runtime tuning touchpoints (KV cache warmup, batching, quantization impact on latency). Actionable next steps include benchmark plan, network config exchange, and PrivateLink onboarding doc.

Topics covered:
- PrivateLink endpoint architecture vs NAT egress for model pulls and control plane
- Subnet layout recommendations (management, inference, egress)
- DNS resolution and split-horizon for internal registry access
- KV cache warmup strategies and p99 impact for cold starts
- Batching sizing guidance for latency SLOs and throughput economics
- Quantization tradeoffs (8-bit/4-bit) and kernel impacts on p50/p95
- Observability: tracing hooks, audit logs, and network flow logs

Shared artifacts referenced:
- Redwood private onboarding doc: https://redwood.example.com/docs/private-onboarding.pdf
- Suggested network diagram: https://redwood.example.com/diagrams/glacier-vpc.pdf
- Benchmark harness + configs (will be shared as gist)

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Samira: all right everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to make sure we got into the network nitty-gritty — um — "PrivateLink and egress tradeoffs". Diego's gonna lead the runtime perf bits, I'm gonna walk through the PrivateLink flow.
[00:00:18] Michael: cool, thanks. we gave folks the calendar note, um timeline's tight for us — want to understand warm start overhead 'cause our SLAs are pretty tight around p95.
[00:00:29] Diego: yeah p95 is the big one. quick note — we'll talk about KV cache, we sometimes see 20-40ms added on first requests if the cache isn't warmed, depends on sequence length.
[00:00:45] Tom: when you say cache, you mean the KV cache on the GPU process? like the key/value attention cache?
[00:00:51] Diego: correct. sometimes folks call it K V cache in notes, transcription stuff, but yes the attention KV cache we keep in GPU memory, the issue is when a request hits a new shard or a newly started pod you get a miss and that can add a chunk while we rehydrate from the prefix or from longer context.
[00:01:10] Asha: how much of that is a network pull though? like if the cache is backed by S3 or object store for cold pods, that'll add network egress to public S3?
[00:01:20] Priya: good question. Redwood's recommended pattern for Private deployments is to pre-pull model artifacts into an internal registry in your VPC or on an NFS accessible from the inference subnet so the model load isn't hitting public egress. We also support direct mounting for on-prem.
[00:01:38] Diego: yep, and for model weights we suggest either local disk on the node or a high-throughput internal object store. If you have to go to public S3, that's where PrivateLink or NAT choices matter.
[00:01:48] Michael: can you contrast PrivateLink vs NAT egress for us? specifically for control plane calls and model pulls.
[00:01:56] Samira: sure. PrivateLink creates an interface endpoint inside your subnet that maps to our service in your region — traffic never leaves the AWS network and you avoid public internet. NAT egress means your inference subnets route through a NAT gateway or instance to reach Redwood's public endpoints. NAT is simpler but you get egress IPs and need to manage firewall rules; PrivateLink is a bit more setup but gives tighter control and avoids public egress.
[00:02:22] Tom: how about DNS? we have split-horizon DNS for internal registries, will PrivateLink complicate resolution?
[00:02:30] Priya: typically you create an interface endpoint and then either use the AWS-provided DNS name (which resolves to the endpoint IPs inside the VPC) or you create private hosted zones to map your internal names. The tricky bit is if you use a corporate proxy that does TLS interception, certificate pinning or SNI routing for traffic — that needs to be accounted for.
[00:02:51] Lance: and for mTLS? our infra team requires mutual TLS to the control plane for audit reasons.
[00:02:56] Samira: we support mTLS for the Private control plane and you can bring your certificates via KMS/HSM integrations. we'll share the runbook.
[00:03:04] Michael: any constraints on subnets? like do you recommend separate subnets for management/control traffic and the inference workers?
[00:03:11] Diego: yes, common pattern: management/controlplane subnet for the Redwood agent and control comms, inference subnets for worker pods with no public IPs, and an egress subnet that houses the NAT or egress appliances. That helps with least privilege routing.
[00:03:26] Tom: if we put the inference pods in private subnets with no route to internet, can they still fetch model updates?
[00:03:33] Priya: only if you provide an internal source — either a VPC endpoint to your object store, an internal registry, or you route via NAT/PrivateLink. We generally recommend model pull before the pod is marked ready: prefetch during image startup on the node so the runtime doesn't block.
[00:03:48] Diego: on the runtime side, for throughputs: batching buys you tokens/sec but hurts tail latency. We suggest dynamic batching with conservative max batch size for p99-sensitive paths. For example for a 1.5B-ish model, batch size of 8-16 may be ideal depending on seq length and hardware.
[00:04:08] Michael: do you have concrete numbers we can baseline? p50/p95/p99 on a dedicated A10 or H100?
[00:04:16] Diego: we can share a benchmark matrix — ballpark, on H100 for a 7B model at 512 tokens: p50 ~ 12-15ms per token, p95 around 60-80ms per request depending on batching and cache warm state. But that's very workload-dependent; we'll run the harness against your expected seq distribution.
[00:04:35] Asha: what about quantization? will a 4-bit quantized model shift those numbers?
[00:04:40] Diego: yes quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput; 8-bit is lowest-risk, 4-bit gives more gains but may require different kernels and can have slight quality delta. The kernel selection in our runtime will pick optimized paths; sometimes 4-bit on specific hardware needs fp16 fallback for certain ops. We'll recommend a quantization profile per model.
[00:04:59] Tom: network egress costs are big for us. Does PrivateLink avoid data transfer charges?
[00:05:04] Samira: PrivateLink still uses AWS networking and there are data processing charges for interface endpoints, but you avoid public internet data transfer egress charges to the internet, and you can keep traffic within region. The cost model differs — we'll provide a cost comparison based on your traffic.
[00:05:18] Michael: ok. on the observability front — we need audit logs, token-level cost breakdown and per-request tracing tied to spans in our system. how does that attach when traffic is over PrivateLink?
[00:05:29] Priya: logs are delivered to your logging endpoint or S3 — on Private deployments we can stream audit logs to your Kinesis/Firehose or S3 in your VPC. For tracing, Redwood emits trace headers that you can correlate; if you're running a local tracer collector we can forward spans via your internal collector. All of this works over PrivateLink as long as the endpoints are configured.
[00:05:47] Lance: and is there anything special about TLS termination? where does it happen?
[00:05:51] Samira: with PrivateLink the TLS terminates at our service but the network path stays private. For mutual TLS setups you can negotiate mTLS at the application layer and present client certs. We also support IP allowlists if you want an extra layer.
[00:06:05] Tom: for NAT setup — is a single NAT gateway per AZ recommended? or NAT instance? we have lots of egress-heavy jobs and worried about bottleneck.
[00:06:13] Priya: best practice is NAT gateway per AZ for high availability and throughput. NAT instances can be tuned but are operational burden. For high egress volumes, an egress proxy cluster (in a separate egress subnet) with autoscaling and egress IP rotation is an option.
[00:06:29] Diego: from runtime perspective, avoid long TCP setup times during model loads: reuse connections, keep-alive at the OS level, and pre-warm certain endpoints. That helps shave tens to hundreds of ms on cold sequences.
[00:06:42] Michael: for the benchmark — what metrics do you need from us to run a realistic test?
[00:06:47] Diego: request size/seq length distribution, expected qps, percent of requests that are short vs long, target SLOs (p50/p95/p99), and whether you plan to use streaming. Also which quant profile to test.
[00:06:59] Asha: we will have mixed traffic — 60% short (<=64 tokens), 30% medium, 10% long. Target p95 latency under 300ms for short. QPS steady state ~120 rps.
[00:07:10] Diego: great that's actionable. We'll run the harness with warm and cold pod scenarios and compute cost per 1M tokens across batching profiles.
[00:07:19] Samira: a few gotchas from other customers: if your DNS resolver or proxy rewrites hostnames, PrivateLink can be unforgiving because it expects the right virtual host header; test with DNS stub resolvers and the actual egress topology.
[00:07:34] Tom: got it. how do we manage cert rotation for mTLS with KMS? we run HashiCorp Vault on prem right now.
[00:07:42] Priya: we can integrate with Vault for cert management, or you can use AWS KMS/HSM. We'll provide a hookup guide, basically Redwood will accept a CA bundle and rotated certs via our onboarding API or via SSM parameter store integration in Private deploys.
[00:07:58] Michael: any special notes about kernel selection and model packaging that affect networking?
[00:08:03] Diego: kernel selection is mostly CPU/GPU-local concern but it affects memory footprint and thus cold-start time — smaller footprint lower download time. So package sizes matter; use sharded weights to parallelize pulls if your network supports it. That reduces wall-clock model load time.
[00:08:17] Lance: sharded pulls — are those multiple parallel GETs to object store, that could hammer our NAT if we don't route carefully?
[00:08:23] Diego: yes exactly — if you do 16 parallel shards and you're routing via a single NAT gateway with limited bandwidth you could saturate it. So plan shard concurrency relative to egress capacity per AZ. Alternatively use a local artifact cache.
[00:08:38] Asha: question on KV cache consistency — if we have multiple replicas serving same model, do you replicate KV cache across pods or is it per-pod and rebuilt on demand?
[00:08:48] Diego: per-pod. We don't replicate KV cache across GPUs live. We rely on prefix caching and sticky routing to keep long-running sessions on same shard. For multi-replica high availability we recommend sticky session routing or client-side affinity to minimize cross-pod misses.
[00:09:02] Michael: sticky routing for sessions — do you offer a route table that pins by conversation id?
[00:09:07] Priya: Redwood routing policies can include user/session hash affinity. For Dedicated/Private deployments you can set session affinity or allow smart routing policies. We'll send a sample config.
[00:09:17] Tom: our security folks care about egress auditability — can we get per-request network flow logs tied to requests?
[00:09:24] Samira: yes we can correlate request ids with network logs. On Private deployments we output request IDs and map them to our trace IDs; you can ingest both sides and correlate in your SIEM. We'll include a mapping guide.
[00:09:37] Lance: are there recommended packet capture points if we need to do a deeper network forensics during pilot?
[00:09:43] Priya: egress proxy nodes, NAT gateway flow logs (VPC Flow Logs), and your internal load balancer are the key spots. We'll advise a short runbook for capturing pcap on the egress cluster.
[00:09:56] Michael: what's the onboarding timeline for PrivateLink? I know some teams saw a week of setup and testing.
[00:10:02] Samira: typical is 3-7 business days for initial infra config + cert exchange; then a week of integration testing, dependent on your internal change window. If you need faster, we can run a temporary NAT-based pilot and swap to PrivateLink later.
[00:10:17] Tom: can we start with NAT pilot and then migrate to PrivateLink with minimal disruption?
[00:10:21] Samira: yes that's a common path. We'll deliver a migration playbook: flip DNS entries or shift route table, and the runtime will re-establish connections gracefully.
[00:10:31] Asha: one more on cost — when you quote dedicated capacity, does that include egress charges?
[00:10:36] Samira: dedicated capacity pricing covers compute and Redwood control plane; network egress in your cloud account is separate. For marketplace/private deployments we can include estimates but the bill is still in your account.
[00:10:47] Diego: circling back to runtime tuning: for your mix (60% short) we should tune batch timeout low so short requests don't wait. Use dynamic batching with a small max batch and 8ms or similar batching window to keep p95 under target. We'll load test to find sweet spot.
[00:11:03] Michael: will you also test with streaming responses? some of our UX uses server-sent-events which changes timing characteristics.
[00:11:08] Diego: yes streaming changes latency profile — early token latency matters more. We'll include both streaming and non-streaming scenarios in the harness.
[00:11:16] Samira: ok let's capture next steps — Diego will produce benchmark harness and initial configs, I'll send PrivateLink checklist and the network diagram, Asha will share the current routing/NAT details.
[00:11:28] Michael: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[00:11:33] Tom: just noting — maybe a quick follow-up doc on shard concurrency vs NAT throughput would be super helpful.
[00:11:38] Diego: yes I'll add a short section in the benchmark doc about shard concurrency and recommended max parallel pulls per NAT instance.
[00:11:45] Samira: perfect, we'll follow up via the CRM thread and create a workback for the pilot. thanks all.

(end of recording)
